common_name: Comanche Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Comanche is an early-blooming, cold-hardy cultivar with tenuifolia heritage.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Comanche, bred by Bigger in 1965, is a dark rose Japanese-form peony with a multicolor staminode center, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2009. Its fern-leaf (tenuifolia) heritage contributes to an attractively fine-textured foliage and a reliably early bloom time. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Coral 'n Gold Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Coral 'n Gold bears large, cupped single flowers prized for their coral tone.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Coral 'n Gold, bred by Cousins and introduced by R.G. Klehm in 1981, bears large, cupped single flowers in a distinctive coral tone, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2009. Single-form peonies like this one show off their golden stamens prominently and tend to need less staking than heavy double forms. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Early Scout Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Early Scout blooms earlier than most garden peonies thanks to its tenuifolia (fern-leaf) parentage.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Early Scout, bred by Auten in 1952, bears very early, dark red single flowers on a plant carrying fern-leaf (tenuifolia) heritage, both won the American Peony Society's Gold Medal in 2001 and its Award of Landscape Merit in 2009. Its early bloom window extends the peony season ahead of most standard lactiflora cultivars, and its finely cut foliage adds ornamental value even after flowering finishes. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Eliza Lundy Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Eliza Lundy is a compact dwarf cultivar reaching only about 22 inches tall.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Eliza Lundy, bred by Krekler in 1975, is a deep red bomb-form peony on a compact dwarf plant only about 22 inches tall, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2011. Its smaller stature suits a front-of-border placement where taller peonies would overwhelm the scale, and the dense bomb-form blooms need less staking than many full-size double cultivars. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Ellen Cowley Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Ellen Cowley was a Grand Champion at the Moscow Peony Show in the 1970s.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Ellen Cowley, bred by Saunders in 1940, bears a warm, light red semi-double flower that earned Grand Champion honors at the Moscow Peony Show for three consecutive years, 1975-1977, and later the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2009. Its semi-double form shows prominent golden stamens alongside the broad petals, giving it a lighter, less top-heavy look than full double cultivars. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Friendship Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Friendship bears a chalky, cool-pink single flower.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Friendship, bred by Glasscock and Falk in 1955, bears a chalky, cool-toned pink single flower, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2012. Its single form shows off prominent golden stamens and needs less staking than heavy double cultivars, holding up well through rain and wind. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Garden Lace Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Garden Lace is a fragrant Japanese-form pink peony.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Garden Lace, bred by Hollingsworth in 1992, bears fragrant, pink, Japanese-form flowers with a delicate, lacy petaloid center, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2014. Its fragrance and softer, less congested flower form make it a good cut-flower choice alongside its garden merit. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Little Red Gem Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Little Red Gem is a very-early, dwarf red single peony growing only about 15 inches tall.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Little Red Gem, bred by D.L. Reath in 1988, is a very-early, dwarf red single peony growing only about 15 inches tall, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2010. Its diminutive scale and early bloom window make it a good choice for a front-of-border or rock-garden placement where larger peonies would be out of proportion. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Lovely Rose Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Lovely Rose bears a creamy salmon-pink semi-double flower.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Lovely Rose, bred by Saunders in 1942, bears a creamy salmon-pink semi-double flower, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2009. Its semi-double form shows some golden stamens through the petals, giving it a slightly lighter appearance than fully double cultivars, with good stem strength for garden display. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Mahogany Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Mahogany is a dark red hybrid peony in the Japanese-form style.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Mahogany, bred by Glasscock in 1937, is a dark red Japanese-form hybrid peony, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2011. Its deep, rich coloring and semi-open center of narrow petaloids distinguish it from the fully double red peonies more commonly grown. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: May Lilac Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Selection)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; May Lilac bears a lavender single flower in early season.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. May Lilac, bred by Saunders in 1950, bears a lavender single flower, selected for the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2022. Its single flower form shows prominent golden stamens and holds up well through spring rain and wind, needing less staking than full double cultivars. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Many Happy Returns Peony (Gold Medal and Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Many Happy Returns is prized for its spectral-red bomb-form blooms and known rebloom tendency.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Many Happy Returns, bred by Hollingsworth in 1986, bears spectral-red, bomb-form flowers and won both the American Peony Society's Gold Medal in 2007 and its Award of Landscape Merit in 2009, a rare double honor reflecting both exhibition quality and garden performance. Its name references a tendency toward a light rebloom later in the season under good conditions, a bonus beyond the typical single spring flush. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Merry Mayshine Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Merry Mayshine carries fern-leaf (tenuifolia) heritage and blooms early.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Merry Mayshine, bred across generations by Saunders, Hollingsworth, and Smetana and introduced in 1994, bears crimson single flowers over finely cut, fern-like foliage from its tenuifolia parentage. It won the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit, valued both for its early bloom and the attractive texture its foliage adds to the garden after flowering finishes. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Minnie Shaylor Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Minnie Shaylor grows unusually tall, to about 38 inches, and may need staking.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, providing support for the tall stems. Minnie Shaylor, bred by Shaylor in 1919, bears a semi-double flower that opens pink and fades to white as it ages, carried on unusually tall stems reaching about 38 inches, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit. Its height and the gradual color shift of individual blooms give it a dynamic presence in the border through its bloom period. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Nice Gal Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Nice Gal bears a rosy-pink, silver-frosted semi-double flower.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Nice Gal, bred by Krekler in 1965, bears a rosy-pink semi-double flower with a distinctive silver-frosted sheen on the petals, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit. The subtle frosted effect catches the light differently than a flat pink color, giving the flowers added depth in the garden. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Roselette Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Roselette carries Paeonia macrophylla heritage and blooms early, with a warm pink single flower.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Roselette, bred by Saunders in 1950, bears an early, warm-pink single flower drawing on Paeonia macrophylla parentage, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit. Its early bloom extends the garden peony season, and the single form shows off golden stamens while needing little staking. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Rozella Peony (Gold Medal Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Rozella is a dark pink rose-form double peony and a 2026 Gold Medal winner.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Rozella, bred by D.L. Reath in 1990, bears a dark pink, rose-form double flower, winning the American Peony Society's Gold Medal in 2026, the Society's highest exhibition honor. Rose-form doubles like this one build their petals in overlapping whorls reminiscent of a classic rose bloom, distinct from the looser bomb or Japanese forms. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Salmon Dream Peony (Gold Medal Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Salmon Dream bears a light salmon semi-double flower.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Salmon Dream, bred by D.L. Reath in 1979, bears a light salmon semi-double flower, winning the American Peony Society's Gold Medal in 2008, the Society's highest exhibition honor. The soft salmon tone is relatively uncommon among peonies, which more often run toward pink, white, or red, giving this cultivar a distinct color niche in the garden. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Scarlett O'Hara Peony (Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Scarlett O'Hara bears a very large scarlet single flower.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Scarlett O'Hara, bred by Glasscock and Falk in 1956, bears a very large, bright scarlet single flower, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit. Its single form and bold scarlet color make it a strong focal point in the border, with sturdy stems that need less staking than full double cultivars of similar flower size. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: The Mackinac Grand Peony (Gold Medal Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; The Mackinac Grand bears a brilliant red semi-double flower.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. The Mackinac Grand, bred by D.L. Reath in 1992, bears a brilliant red semi-double flower, winning the American Peony Society's Gold Medal in 2013, the Society's highest exhibition honor. Its vivid, saturated red color and well-formed semi-double blooms have made it a standout exhibition and garden cultivar in the decades since its introduction. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Topeka Garnet Peony (Gold Medal Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; Topeka Garnet bears a dark red single flower.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Topeka Garnet, bred by Bigger in 1975, bears a dark red single flower, winning the American Peony Society's Gold Medal in 2012, the Society's highest exhibition honor. Its deep garnet-red color and clean single form give it a bold, saturated presence in the garden, with prominent golden stamens typical of single-form peonies. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Charm Peony (1931 Franklin Hybrid, Award of Landscape Merit Winner)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil; this 1931 Charm is a distinct herbaceous hybrid, not to be confused with later peonies sharing the same cultivar name.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. This Charm, bred by Franklin in 1931, is a dark red Japanese-form peony with a satiny petal finish, earning the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit in 2009. The cultivar name 'Charm' has been reused across the peony world for several distinct cultivars over the decades, including Red Charm, Coral Charm, Border Charm, and Prairie Charm already in wide cultivation, so this 1931 Franklin-bred plant is a historically distinct, earlier introduction under the same bare name. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover.
